# The T1w/T2w Ratio for Myelin Mapping {.unnumbered}

{{< include "../includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

A recurring goal of quantitative MRI is a map of myelin content. One popular and inexpensive approach was proposed based on using only two ordinary structural scans — a T1-weighted and a  T2-weighted image. The idea was to take the ratio of these two images in the hope that this would be a measure of myelination. 

This resource describes the idea and, importantly, the why it should not be considered as a myelin measure.

## The idea

The T1w/T2w method was introduced by Glasser and Van Essen (2011) as a way to map cortical areas from myelin content (@fig-t1t2-glasser-vanessen). In fact, they refer to the method as myelin mapping.

The idea of the method is that by taking the ratio of these two images, a space-varying bias of the MR images is eliminated. Namely, the MR receive-coil sensitivity varies as we measure across the brain volume.  The excite-coil differences are less severe because excitation is typically performed by the whole body coil.

The T1-weighted and a T2-weighted images both carry a similar receive-coil intensity bias. After all, they are measured using the same coils.  If we take the *ratio*, the receive-coil bias divides out. When measuring the white matter, the thinking goes, the biggest image contrast will be due to myelin. Thus, Glasser and Van Essen suggested that the resulting T1w/T2w maps are essentially measurements of myelin contrast.

The attractive feature of these T1w/T2w ratios (myelin maps) is the ease of their implementation. 3T scanners and pulse sequences can all make such measurements from standard sequences, without any special pulse sequence development. Support for the idea came from the observation that when these data are mapped to the cortical surface, the spatial gradients of the group map agree well with cytoarchitectonic areal borders. So the ratio became a widely used, low-cost proxy for cortical myelination.  Other, more biologically based gold-standard methods exist but the measurements are difficult to make and analyze.  Anyone who can divide can make this measurement.

![Glasser and Van Essen (2011) introduced the T1w/T2w ratio to map cortical areas
by myelin content; the ratio cancels the shared receive-coil intensity bias.](images/t1t2-ratio-glasser-vanessen.png){#fig-t1t2-glasser-vanessen}

## Why the ratio is not a specific myelin measure

The convenience of the method should not be mistaken for validity. A series of
studies comparing the T1w/T2w ratio against histology and against more direct
myelin-MRI measures — quantitative susceptibility mapping, magnetization transfer
saturation, and multi-echo myelin water fraction (MWF) — find that the ratio does
not track myelin specifically, especially in white matter
(@fig-t1t2-critique-1, @fig-t1t2-critique-2).

Several findings recur across this literature. In the corpus callosum the T1w/T2w map does not positively correlate with Luxol-fast-blue optical density and shows, if anything, a weak negative correlation, whereas myelin water fraction correlates strongly and positively with the histology. Direct method comparisons find only weak correlations between the T1w/T2w ratio and both SyMRI relaxometry and MT saturation, even though those two agree well with each other. 

![Studies reporting a discrepancy between T1w/T2w maps and histology, and weak
correlations with other myelin-MRI measures.](images/t1t2-ratio-critique-1.png){#fig-t1t2-critique-1}

And reliability is not the issue — the ratio is highly reproducible test–retest — but reproducibility is not validity: a measure can be stable yet still fail to reflect the quantity of
interest. The reasonable summary is that the T1w/T2w ratio may correlate with myelin at the cortical level but is not a specific map of myelin density in white matter, and should be used with that limitation in mind.

![Test–retest and concurrent-validity comparisons: the T1w/T2w ratio is reliable
but has low criterion validity as an index of myelin, particularly in white and
subcortical structures.](images/t1t2-ratio-critique-2.png){#fig-t1t2-critique-2}
